body:
Points, Lines, Rays and Angles: 1. Drawings labeled; a ray has one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction, while a line goes on forever in both directions and has no endpoints. 2. Right = 90 degrees (square corner); acute < 90 degrees; obtuse between 90 and 180 degrees. 3. Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never meet; perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. 4. 90 degrees. 5. 180 degrees. 6. A right angle; 90 degrees. 7. Examples: the corner of a book or the door (right angle); the opposite edges of a window or the lines on notebook paper (parallel).
Measuring and Adding Angles: 1. A 40-degree angle, checked with a protractor (accept 38 to 42). 2. A 125-degree angle (accept 123 to 127); obtuse. 3. 90 − 35 = 55 degrees. 4. 180 − 60 − 45 = 75 degrees. 5. 95 + x = 150; x = 55 degrees. 6. 360 ÷ 8 = 45 degrees. 7. Line up the center mark on the vertex and the 0 line on one ray, then read the row that starts at 0 on that ray; check that an acute angle reads less than 90.
Sorting Shapes and Finding Symmetry: 1. Square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram always have two pairs of parallel sides; a trapezoid is only sure to have at least one pair. 2. A right triangle. 3. No: two right angles already make 180 degrees, so the other two sides would be parallel and could never meet to close the triangle. 4. Examples: a rectangle or square has perpendicular sides; an equilateral triangle or a regular hexagon has none. 5. Square 4; rectangle 2; equilateral triangle 3; A 1; H 2; F 0. 6. Examples: an isosceles triangle, a heart, the letter A, a kite, with the line drawn correctly. 7. Yes: a square has four right angles and two pairs of parallel sides, which is everything a rectangle needs; it also has equal sides.
Geometry Check: 1. A labeled ray (one endpoint), line segment (two endpoints) and perpendicular lines (meeting at a right angle). 2. Acute, right, obtuse. 3. A 70-degree angle (accept 68 to 72). 4. 180 − 112 = 68 degrees, or 112 + a = 180, a = 68. 5. 45 degrees. 6. A rectangle. 7. Regular hexagon 6; M 1; Z 0. 8. A right triangle. No: the other two angles must add to 90 degrees, so neither can be more than 90.
Scoring tip: allow 2 degrees either way on drawn angles; on the precision criterion, a measure without the word degrees or the degree symbol is Developing.
